title: Lingerie Stores
one_liner: Specialty lingerie stores sell bras, panties, shapewear, sleepwear and related intimate apparel, competing on fit, brand, assortment and omnichannel convenience.
overview: This industry covers retailers whose main business is intimate apparel, including bras, panties, lingerie, shapewear, sleepwear and adjacent categories such as swim. The 2021 IBIS baseline described a $6.213 billion specialty-store industry that had been hurt by COVID-19 store closures, mall traffic declines and online competition, but supported by rising disposable income, plus-size demand and better fitting services. In current 2025 data, the broader U.S. lingerie market is estimated at $17.95 billion, while an implied specialty-store channel opportunity is about $7.2 billion using the 2025 North American specialty-store share of 40.27%. The industry remains concentrated around Victoria's Secret and PINK, but growth is increasingly influenced by Aerie, Skims, ThirdLove, Savage X Fenty, Bare Necessities and mass retailers with strong online reach.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 U.S. lingerie stores addressable specialty-channel sales estimated at about $7.2 billion, inferred from Grand View Research's 2025 U.S. lingerie market value of $17.95 billion and Mordor Intelligence's 2025 North American specialty-store distribution share of 40.27%.
key_stats.growth: 2025-2033 U.S. all-channel lingerie market CAGR forecast at 7.2%; online channel forecast at 7.8% CAGR, while specialty stores remained the largest North American distribution channel in 2025.
key_stats.broader_market: 2025 U.S. all-channel lingerie market: $17.95 billion; 2024: $17.11 billion.
key_stats.major_player_sales: Victoria's Secret & Co. fiscal 2025 net sales were $6.553 billion, up 5.2% from fiscal 2024, with North America store sales of $3.5445 billion, up 3.4%.
key_stats.stores: Victoria's Secret & Co. ended fiscal 2025 on January 31, 2026 with 766 U.S. company-operated stores and 790 company-operated North America stores.
key_stats.consumer_income_driver: U.S. per-capita disposable personal income was $66,871 in 2025, up from $64,446 in 2024 and $56,559 in 2022.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 specialty-store revenue baseline estimated at $6.28 billion, derived from the IBIS 2021 revenue figure of $6.213 billion and its 2021-2027 projected CAGR of 1.06%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 growth baseline: +1.06% projected annual growth from the 2021 IBIS forecast path.
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 2021 IBIS baseline profit margin was 6.3%; the baseline projected profit rising slightly to 6.4% of revenue by 2026.
baseline_2022.wages: 2021 IBIS baseline wages were $948 million, equal to 15.3% of industry revenue.
baseline_2022.establishments: 2021 IBIS baseline establishments were 15,847 locations and enterprises were 14,170.

how_it_makes_money: Stores earn revenue by selling bras, panties, shapewear, sleepwear, hosiery, swim and related intimate apparel through owned stores, outlet stores, e-commerce sites, marketplaces and loyalty programs. Higher-margin sales come from private-label brands, bra fitting services, premium materials, fashion collections, replenishment basics, bundles, subscriptions and cross-selling beauty, lounge, swim and activewear.
cost_structure: Merchandise purchases and buying/occupancy costs are the largest expense category, followed by store labor, rent, distribution, e-commerce fulfillment, marketing and corporate overhead. The 2021 IBIS baseline put wages at 15.3% of revenue and profit at 6.3% of revenue. Current public filings show pressure from imported-product costs: Victoria's Secret reported about $85 million of tariff pressure in fiscal 2025, and AEO said tariff impact reduced fourth-quarter 2025 gross margin by about 280 basis points.
major_players: AEO Inc. / Aerie and OFFLINE by Aerie
current_dynamics: The category has shifted from occasion-led lingerie toward daily comfort, fit, shapewear, lounge and active-adjacent intimates. Specialty stores still have an advantage in bra fitting, brand experience and high-margin private label, but online specialists and marketplaces have normalized buying bras and shapewear without visiting a store. Victoria's Secret's 2025 rebound shows that large store fleets can still generate growth when merchandising, brand marketing and omnichannel execution improve. At the same time, tariffs, higher inventory costs and value-conscious consumers are forcing more careful pricing and promotion.
whats_growing: Comfort bras, bralettes, wireless styles, shapewear, inclusive and extended sizing, maternity and post-pregnancy intimates, men's and gender-inclusive adjacent basics, premium everyday underwear, digital fit tools, loyalty-driven replenishment, online sales and omnichannel pickup/return behavior are growing. Aerie's fiscal 2025 revenue rose 12% to $1.9 billion, and its first-quarter 2026 revenue rose 34% year over year, signaling continued consumer demand for comfort-led and inclusive positioning.
whats_shrinking: Traditional mall-only lingerie formats, formal hosiery, narrow-size assortments, heavily sexualized legacy positioning, undifferentiated midprice stores and low-service specialty shops are losing ground. Victoria's Secret reduced its U.S. company-operated store base from 782 at February 1, 2025 to 766 at January 31, 2026, showing ongoing pruning even during a sales recovery.
recent_developments: June 2023: Victoria's Secret expanded onto Amazon Fashion with more than 4,000 Victoria's Secret and PINK items, accelerating marketplace competition for specialty stores.
May 2, 2025: U.S. tariff changes ended de minimis duty-free treatment for China-origin low-value shipments, raising landed-cost pressure for direct-to-consumer apparel sellers.
March 5, 2026: Victoria's Secret reported fiscal 2025 net sales of $6.553 billion, up 5.2%, and fiscal 2025 comparable sales up 5%.
March 5, 2026: Victoria's Secret said fiscal 2025 adjusted operating income was $403 million despite about $85 million of tariff pressure.
March 4, 2026: AEO reported Aerie fiscal 2025 revenue of $1.935 billion, up 12%, with Aerie comparable sales up 9%.
June 2, 2026: Victoria's Secret reported first-quarter 2026 net sales of $1.560 billion, up 15%, and raised fiscal 2026 net sales guidance to $7.030-$7.130 billion.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is modestly positive for well-capitalized specialty retailers and harder for small store operators. Demand should be supported by 2025 income growth, replenishment needs, comfort-led product cycles and size inclusivity, while online growth continues to outpace the total market. Store fleets are likely to be more selective, with closures of weak mall locations offset by better productivity, shop-in-shop formats, outlets and omnichannel services. Margin risk remains elevated because intimate apparel is import-heavy, and 2025-2026 tariff changes add cost pressure that may be passed through only partly to consumers.
one_sentence: The U.S. lingerie-store industry is mature but improving in 2025-2026 as Victoria's Secret, Aerie and digital-native brands benefit from comfort-led replenishment, inclusive sizing and better omnichannel execution while tariff costs, mall exposure and online competition pressure margins.

title: Lipstick Manufacturing
one_liner: U.S. lipstick manufacturers blend color cosmetics, therapeutic balms and hybrid lip-care products for beauty retailers, mass merchants, drugstores, department stores and brand-owned channels.
overview: Lipstick Manufacturing covers the preparation, blending, compounding and packaging of lipsticks, glosses, balms, stains, liners and related lip-care products in the United States. The baseline report sized 2021 revenue at $3.972 billion and projected a rebound to about $4.6 billion by 2026 as post-pandemic makeup usage, premium beauty and product innovation recovered. Current 2025-2026 market signals are mixed but constructive: Circana reported 2025 U.S. prestige beauty sales of $36.0 billion, up 4.0% year over year, and mass beauty sales of $72.7 billion, up 5.0%; within makeup, lip products were among the clearest growth contributors in both prestige and mass channels.

key_stats.market_size: 2026 projected U.S. lipstick manufacturing revenue: about $4.6 billion, from the baseline 2021-2026 forecast.
key_stats.growth: 2021-2026 projected industry revenue CAGR: +3.0% per year in the baseline forecast.
key_stats.profit_margin: 2021 industry profit margin: 6.1%; 2026 projected profit margin: 6.2% in the baseline forecast.
key_stats.employment: 2026 projected industry employment: 5,073 workers, from the baseline 2021-2026 forecast.
key_stats.enterprises: 2026 projected industry enterprises: 88 operators, from the baseline 2021-2026 forecast.
key_stats.trade: 2026 projected industry imports: $483.9 million; 2026 projected exports: $297.0 million in the baseline forecast.
key_stats.retail_context: 2025 U.S. prestige beauty retail sales: $36.0 billion, up 4.0%; 2025 U.S. mass beauty retail sales: $72.7 billion, up 5.0%, according to Circana.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 estimated U.S. lipstick manufacturing revenue: about $4.09 billion, calculated from 2021 revenue of $3.972 billion and the baseline 2021-2026 CAGR of +3.0%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 estimated industry revenue growth: +3.0% year over year, based on the baseline 2021-2026 forecast path.
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 2022 estimated profit margin: about 6.1%, consistent with the baseline forecast of 6.1% in 2021 and 6.2% in 2026.
baseline_2022.context: 2022 was the first full year after the 2021 reopening rebound, with demand shifting back toward makeup occasions while lip balm and natural-positioned products retained pandemic-era momentum.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue by selling finished lip products and private-label or contract-manufactured runs to beauty specialty chains, mass merchants, drugstores, department stores, e-commerce retailers, brand owners and wholesalers. Higher margins come from premium lipsticks, luxury glosses, long-wear stains, lip oils, tinted balms and skincare-benefit hybrids, while volume comes from mass lip balm, gloss, liner and replenishment products.

cost_structure.materials_and_packaging: 2025-2026 costs are driven by waxes, oils, pigments, emollients, active skincare ingredients, fragrance/flavor inputs, tubes, cartons, labels and secondary packaging; tariff uncertainty and imported ingredient exposure remain current cost risks.
cost_structure.wages: 2021 wages were 7.0% of revenue in the baseline report, with 2026 wages projected to rise at a 2.7% annual rate over 2021-2026 as R&D, testing and marketing-support roles expand.
cost_structure.profit: 2021 average profit was 6.1% of revenue, with 2026 profit projected at 6.2% as premium mix offsets higher R&D, compliance and promotional spending.
cost_structure.marketing_and_r_and_d: 2025-2026 spending is concentrated on rapid launches, influencer and social content, claims substantiation, clean/vegan/natural formulations, shade expansion and skincare-benefit innovation.
cost_structure.compliance: 2026 costs include MoCRA facility-registration renewals, product listings, ingredient documentation, adverse-event systems and stronger quality records for cosmetic manufacturers and responsible persons.

major_players: L'Oreal USA: Major U.S. beauty manufacturer with Maybelline, NYX Professional Makeup and L'Oreal Paris lip products; L'Oreal reported $11B+ U.S. revenue in 2025 and highlighted NYX Lip IV and Maybelline lip-tint innovation in 2025.

The Estee Lauder Companies: Prestige beauty owner of MAC, Clinique, Bobbi Brown and Tom Ford Beauty; fiscal 2025 makeup sales declined 6.0% globally, but Clinique and hero franchises helped offset weakness.
Coty: Owner of CoverGirl, Rimmel and Max Factor; fiscal 2025 Consumer Beauty revenue fell 8.0% to $2.073 billion, with U.S. color-cosmetics softness pressuring CoverGirl and related brands.
Revlon: Longstanding mass color-cosmetics and lipstick brand competing through drug, mass and online channels after post-restructuring portfolio refocus.
e.l.f. Beauty: Fast-growing value-led cosmetics challenger built around eye, lip and face products; fiscal 2025 positioning emphasized clean, vegan, cruelty-free and accessible-price cosmetics.
current_dynamics: The strongest 2025 signal is that lip is outperforming the broader makeup shelf. Circana reported 2025 prestige makeup growth of 4.0%, with lip liner, lip oils and balms among top-gaining segments, and described lip as the fastest-growing makeup segment in mass retail. At the same time, retailers and manufacturers are navigating cautious consumers, price-value convergence between mass and prestige, tariff uncertainty, heavier promotional activity and MoCRA compliance deadlines. The industry is increasingly launch-driven: brands need frequent shade, format and ingredient updates to stay visible on TikTok, Sephora, Ulta, Amazon and mass retail shelves.
whats_growing: 2025 lip liner, driven by contouring and 1990s-inspired social trends; Circana cited lip liner growth of +28% in prestige and +36% in mass so far in 2025.
2025 lip oils, tinted balms and lip treatments, which combine color payoff with skincare benefits and were top gainers in Circana's 2025 beauty readout.
2025 value-oriented prestige and premium-priced mass brands, as consumers compare efficacy and price rather than treating higher price as automatic quality.
2025-2026 private-label, masstige and digitally native brands that can launch fast, test shades socially and scale through Ulta, Target, Amazon and brand DTC channels.
2026 MoCRA-ready manufacturers and contract manufacturers with stronger documentation, ingredient traceability and regulatory systems.
whats_shrinking: 2025 traditional color cosmetics outside high-growth lip formats, with Coty citing negative U.S. color-cosmetics market trends in fiscal 2025.
2025 low-differentiation matte lipstick and gloss SKUs without skincare, long-wear, plumping, clean, vegan or premium-positioned claims.
2025 brands dependent on heavy discounting, as Coty reported fiscal 2025 Consumer Beauty pressure from higher returns, discounts and promotions.
2025 brick-and-mortar-only demand models, as beauty discovery and replenishment keep shifting toward omnichannel retail, social media and e-commerce.
2026 small manufacturers without MoCRA compliance infrastructure, because facility registration, product listings and recordkeeping raise fixed operating burden.
recent_developments: 2025-02-01: Ulta Beauty reported fiscal 2024 cosmetics at 39% of net sales, down from 41% in fiscal 2023, showing category mix pressure despite beauty demand.
2025-06-30: Coty fiscal 2025 Consumer Beauty revenue declined 8.0% to $2.073 billion, citing U.S. color-cosmetics softness affecting CoverGirl, Sally Hansen and Rimmel.
2025-08-19: Circana reported first-half 2025 prestige makeup sales of $5.2 billion, up 1.0%, with lip products the top contributor and the only growth area in mass cosmetics.
2025-09-04: Circana reported lip liner growth of +28% in prestige and +36% in mass so far in 2025, driven by lip contouring and social-media trends.
2026-02-10: Circana reported full-year 2025 prestige beauty sales of $36.0 billion, up 4.0%, and mass beauty sales of $72.7 billion, up 5.0%; lip was the fastest-growing mass makeup segment.
2026-02-11: FDA updated Cosmetics Direct materials for MoCRA biennial facility-registration renewals, reinforcing 2026 compliance work for cosmetic manufacturers.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is moderately positive. The baseline forecast points to about $4.6 billion in 2026 U.S. lipstick manufacturing revenue, with 2021-2026 CAGR of +3.0%. Current 2025 retail data supports that direction because lip is outperforming broader makeup, but growth is likely uneven: premium and hybrid lip-care formats should gain share, while legacy color-cosmetics lines face discounting, weak unit growth and inventory discipline. Margins should stay near the 2021-2026 baseline range of 6.1%-6.2% if manufacturers can pass through ingredient, packaging, compliance and tariff-related costs through premiumization and faster innovation.

title: Lithium Battery Manufacturing
one_liner: U.S. lithium battery manufacturing is scaling fast around EV and grid-storage demand, but margins and utilization are pressured by cheaper Asian supply, slower EV plans, and policy uncertainty.
overview: Lithium Battery Manufacturing in the United States has moved from a niche, import-challenged industry into a strategic manufacturing buildout tied to electric vehicles, utility-scale storage and supply-chain security. The 2020 IBISWorld baseline described a small domestic lithium battery manufacturing industry with 2020 revenue of $1.545 billion and a 2020-2025 forecast CAGR of 3.0%, but newer public and market sources show a much larger lithium-ion battery market by 2025 as domestic cell, module and pack capacity expanded. U.S. demand is still highly exposed to EV sales cycles, battery chemistry shifts, imported cells and components, and federal tax-credit rules, while manufacturing output has increasingly shifted toward downstream cell, module and pack assembly rather than fully domestic active-material supply.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 U.S. lithium-ion battery market revenue: $14.1 billion to $15.6 billion, depending on source and scope
key_stats.growth: 2025-2030 U.S. lithium-ion battery market CAGR: 9.7%; 2026-2034 CAGR: 10.55% in another market estimate
key_stats.manufacturing_capacity: 2024 U.S. battery manufacturing capacity exceeded 200 GWh, with nearly 700 GWh additional capacity under construction
key_stats.employment: 2024 U.S. battery manufacturing employment reached 54,400 workers, the highest recorded level since 1972 for NAICS battery manufacturing
key_stats.battery_price: 2025 average lithium-ion battery pack price fell 8% year over year to $108/kWh
key_stats.grid_storage_demand: 2025 EIA expected 18.2 GW of new U.S. utility-scale battery storage capacity additions

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 implied IBISWorld baseline revenue: about $1.64 billion in 2020 dollars, calculated from 2020 revenue of $1.545 billion and the 2020-2025 forecast CAGR of 3.0%
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 baseline growth assumption: 3.0% annualized revenue growth from the 2020 IBISWorld forecast
baseline_2022.context: 2022 Census/CRS shipment value for domestically produced non-lead-acid energy storage batteries was $16.6 billion, a broader category than the legacy IBISWorld lithium battery manufacturing definition

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell primary lithium batteries, rechargeable lithium-ion cells, modules and packs, plus engineered battery systems and related services. Revenue comes from long-term supply agreements with automakers, energy-storage integrators, electronics and industrial customers, and specialty buyers in defense, medical and microlithium applications. Large plants depend on high utilization, chemistry-specific production lines, yield improvement, and purchase commitments because fixed costs are high and battery prices fall quickly.

cost_structure.materials: Largest cost bucket; lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, copper, aluminum, electrolyte, separators and cathode/anode materials drive bill-of-material exposure.
cost_structure.labor: Skilled production, engineering, maintenance, safety and quality-control labor is rising as U.S. gigafactories hire and train workers.
cost_structure.depreciation_and_capex: Very high; cell plants require multibillion-dollar dry rooms, coating, formation, testing and automation assets.
cost_structure.energy_and_utilities: Material because cell manufacturing is electricity-intensive and requires controlled humidity, thermal management and clean production environments.
cost_structure.r_and_d: High and ongoing for chemistry, yield, energy density, cycle life, safety and manufacturing-process improvements.
cost_structure.profit: Margins are pressured by import competition, customer concentration, ramp-up inefficiency and falling pack prices, partly offset by scale, automation and production credits.

current_dynamics: The U.S. industry is expanding capacity faster than mature domestic upstream supply can support it. Panasonic remained the largest supplier for U.S.-produced electric cars in 2025, while Korean producers such as LG Energy Solution, SK On and Samsung SDI increased U.S. footprints through automaker partnerships. At the same time, automakers have slowed or revised some EV plans, pushing battery producers to reallocate capacity toward LFP and stationary storage. China still dominates global cell production and much of the midstream supply chain, keeping U.S. producers under cost pressure even with tariffs and incentives.
whats_growing: Grid-scale and behind-the-meter storage, LFP batteries for energy storage, domestic cell and module assembly, battery recycling and black-mass processing, workforce training, and localized supply agreements tied to IRA-style domestic-content economics are growing. U.S. utility-scale battery storage additions were expected by EIA to reach 18.2 GW in 2025, creating a second demand leg beyond EVs.
whats_shrinking: Primary disposable lithium batteries are shrinking as a share of industry relevance, while some NMC-focused EV capacity faces weaker utilization because several automakers revised EV timing. Imported low-cost cells remain a threat to domestic share, but tariffs and sourcing rules have reduced some China-linked EV battery demand in the United States. Margins are also shrinking where producers must absorb falling global battery prices and ramp-up costs.
recent_developments: 2025-02-24: EIA expected 18.2 GW of U.S. utility-scale battery storage additions in 2025 after 10.3 GW were added in 2024.
2025-04-09: LG Energy Solution said its Arizona battery complex had reached the halfway construction milestone and was preparing to deliver 46-Series cylindrical batteries in 2026.
2025-07-14: Panasonic Energy began mass production at its De Soto, Kansas lithium-ion battery factory, targeting about 32 GWh of annual capacity.
2025-08-19: BlueOval SK began battery production at its Kentucky 1 facility for the Ford F-150 Lightning.
2025-12-09: BloombergNEF reported average lithium-ion pack prices fell 8% in 2025 to $108/kWh.
2025-12-11: Ford and SK On agreed to separate BlueOval SK operations in 2026, reflecting slower EV demand and revised production plans.
outlook: The 2026-2030 outlook is positive but less linear than the 2021-2023 investment boom implied. Domestic capacity should keep increasing as large plants in Kansas, Kentucky, Tennessee, Arizona, Georgia and other states ramp, and stationary storage gives manufacturers a growing demand channel less dependent on consumer EV adoption. The main risks are underutilized EV-focused lines, changes to federal incentives, high U.S. production costs versus Asia, component import dependence, and battery-price deflation. Companies with secure offtake, LFP capability, strong yields and access to domestic or allied materials are best positioned.
themes: Grid storage as a second growth engine
China cost advantage and trade exposure
one_sentence: The industry makes lithium and lithium-ion cells, modules and packs for vehicles, electronics, industrial equipment and energy storage, with 2025 growth led by domestic gigafactory ramp-ups and stationary storage while EV battery demand becomes more uneven.

title: Livestock Production Support Services in the US
one_liner: A fragmented animal-production services market that is being pulled between shrinking cattle herds, stronger disease surveillance needs and steady equine boarding demand.
overview: The industry is a mature, low-concentration support market tied to livestock farm activity and equine ownership. IBISWorld's 2022 baseline put revenue at $5.2 billion in 2022 after 0.7% annualized growth over 2017-2022 and a 1.1% decline in 2022. Public IBISWorld data later showed revenue at $4.7 billion in 2024 and $4.7 billion in 2025, with a 2.5% annualized decline over 2019-2024 and 1.4% growth in 2024. Current demand is mixed: USDA reported only 86.2 million cattle and calves on US farms as of January 1, 2026, down from 2025, while USDA projected red meat and poultry availability at 226 pounds per person in 2025 and 227 pounds in 2026, supported by chicken and pork rather than beef. The strongest near-term service opportunities are biosecurity, disease testing, traceability, dairy herd monitoring, breeding efficiency, animal health work and equine boarding, while routine outsourced work remains vulnerable when farms bring services in-house.

key_stats.growth: 2019-2024 revenue CAGR of -2.5%; 2024 revenue growth of 1.4%; 2025 revenue approximately flat at $4.7 billion
key_stats.employment: 52.3 thousand jobs in NAICS 115210 in 2025, up 12.2% from 2024 on a BLS productivity basis
key_stats.employer_establishments: 4,791 employer establishments in 2023 Census Business Patterns
key_stats.cattle_inventory: 86.2 million cattle and calves on January 1, 2026, with beef cows at 27.6 million and milk cows at 9.57 million
key_stats.meat_availability: 226 pounds per person of red meat and poultry in 2025 and 227 pounds projected for 2026

baseline_2022.growth: 0.7% annualized revenue growth over 2017-2022, including a 1.1% decline in 2022
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022 revenue mix: boarding services 49.5%, dairy support services 20.5%, breeding services 16.4%, farrier services 6.4%, livestock health services 4.9%, spraying services 1.5%, shearing services 0.8%

how_it_makes_money: Operators earn fees from horse and livestock boarding, breeding and artificial insemination support, pedigree and record services, dairy herd improvement and milk testing, vaccination and animal health support, livestock spraying and parasite control, sheep shearing, farrier work, biosecurity services, movement documentation and other specialized outsourced tasks that farms or animal owners do not perform internally.
cost_structure: The business is labor-heavy and locally delivered. The 2022 baseline showed wages of $1.9 billion on $5.2 billion of revenue, while profit was $391 million and the profit margin was 7.5%. Main costs are skilled labor, subcontracted veterinarians and technicians, animal feed and bedding for boarding operations, insurance, fuel, vehicles, testing supplies, pharmaceuticals, animal handling equipment, rent or facility upkeep, utilities, software and compliance costs. Cost pressure in 2025-2026 is elevated by wage competition, disease-control protocols, insurance, equipment, and the need for electronic identification and testing workflows.
major_players: No major company held enough 2024 market share for IBISWorld to list as a major player
Eurofins DQCI is a notable dairy testing and quality-control participant referenced in the 2022 baseline
The market is dominated by small local owner-operators, equine boarding facilities, breeders, farriers, testing providers and animal-health service firms
current_dynamics: Shrinking cattle inventory is limiting some volume-based service demand, especially for beef cattle support, but high cattle values make producers more willing to pay for services that protect herd health, fertility and traceability. Dairy support is being reshaped by H5N1 surveillance and milk testing under USDA's National Milk Testing Strategy. New World screwworm risk in 2025-2026 has raised demand for inspection, treatment, movement documentation and biosecurity support near cattle and equine supply chains. At the same time, larger farms continue to invest in in-house technology, automated feeding, precision livestock tools, electronic ID and data systems, reducing some outsourcing opportunities.
whats_growing: Biosecurity planning, disease testing, interstate movement compliance, electronic ID and traceability services, dairy herd monitoring, milk testing, vaccination support, parasite surveillance, specialized breeding and genetics services, and premium equine boarding are growing in importance in 2025-2026. Broiler and pork availability growth in 2025-2026 also supports demand for animal-health, productivity and compliance services tied to intensive production systems.
whats_shrinking: Routine cattle support tied to herd expansion is shrinking because USDA reported 86.2 million cattle and calves on January 1, 2026 and beef cows down 1% from 2025. Low-margin outsourced tasks are also under pressure as farms bring services in-house using better access to credit, automation and precision livestock systems. Beef-linked service volume is weaker than poultry and pork-linked demand, and small operators remain exposed to wage, feed, insurance and facility-cost inflation.
recent_developments: 2024-11-05: USDA electronic identification rules took effect requiring visually and electronically readable official eartags for covered cattle and bison moving interstate.
2024-12-06: USDA launched the National Milk Testing Strategy and required raw milk samples to be shared for H5N1 testing upon request.
2025-08-21: USDA ERS projected red meat and poultry availability at 226 pounds per person in 2025 and 227 pounds in 2026.
2026-01-30: USDA NASS reported 86.2 million cattle and calves on US farms as of January 1, 2026, with beef cows down 1% from 2025.
2026-04-20: USDA APHIS listed the National Milk Testing Strategy as the framework for state H5N1 surveillance and dairy herd status.
2026-06-03: USDA APHIS confirmed New World screwworm in a bovine in Zavala County, Texas, with no further detections reported at that announcement.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is cautious. Revenue is likely to remain near the 2025 level of $4.7 billion unless disease-control work and equine services offset the weaker cattle cycle. The 2026 cattle herd remains historically tight, with USDA reporting 86.2 million cattle and calves as of January 1, 2026, so beef-cattle service volume should stay constrained until herd rebuilding begins. However, service intensity per animal is rising because animal disease traceability, H5N1 milk testing, New World screwworm preparedness and precision herd management require specialized labor and equipment. Over 2026-2030, the industry should remain fragmented and slow-growing to slightly declining, with higher-value technical services gaining share and routine labor services facing in-house substitution.

title: Locksmiths
one_liner: A fragmented local-service industry built around lock installation, repair, rekeying, access control, safes, emergency entry and automotive key work.
overview: The Locksmiths industry covers establishments that install, repair, rebuild and adjust mechanical or electronic locking devices, safes and security vaults, often alongside the sale of related hardware. Demand is anchored in commercial facilities, residential turnover, new construction, property management, emergency lockouts, automotive key programming and security upgrades. The industry is local and low-concentration, with many owner-operators and small shops, but service scope is becoming more technical as electronic locks, smart access systems, keyless entry, CCTV-adjacent work and vehicle transponder keys increase the skill and equipment requirements.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: $2.9B according to IBISWorld; 2025: about $3.0B-$3.1B according to Kentley/ResearchAndMarkets public report pages
key_stats.growth: 2025: +1.3% market-size growth according to IBISWorld; 2020-2025: -0.2% CAGR according to IBISWorld; 2020-2025: +5.2% annual growth according to Kentley/ResearchAndMarkets public report pages
key_stats.employment: 2025: 15,040 employed locksmiths and safe repairers in BLS OEWS wage data, excluding many self-employed operators
key_stats.wages: 2025: $26.67 mean hourly wage and $55,470 mean annual wage for locksmiths and safe repairers in BLS OEWS data
key_stats.companies: 2025: 3,861 companies according to Kentley; 2025: 3,837 companies according to ResearchAndMarkets/Kentley listing
key_stats.concentration: 2025: top four companies held 7.2% share according to Kentley public report page
key_stats.construction_driver: 2025: US housing starts totaled 1.36M, down 0.6% from 2024; 2025 permits totaled 1.43M, down 3.6% from 2024
key_stats.housing_turnover_driver: 2025: existing-home sales totaled about 4.061M, roughly flat with 2024 and the lowest annual total since 1995 according to NAR-reported data

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: about $2.88B implied by the baseline IBISWorld 2021 revenue of $2.82B and its 2021-2026 forecast CAGR of 2.1%
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: +2.1% implied baseline forecast growth from IBISWorld's 2021-2026 outlook
baseline_2022.baseline_context: The baseline expected a post-COVID recovery to $3.1B by 2026, supported by housing starts, existing home sales, business formation and private nonresidential construction.

how_it_makes_money: Locksmiths earn revenue from nonresidential lock and access-control installation and repair, residential rekeying and lock installation, emergency lockout calls, automotive key cutting and fob programming, safe and vault servicing, key duplication, security hardware resale, and consulting on physical access systems. The 2021 baseline product mix was 44.1% nonresidential security installation and repair, 24.4% residential installation and repair, 16.5% key cutting and duplication, 10.3% resale of locks/security merchandise, 1.7% monitored system services and 3.0% other services.
cost_structure: Labor is the main cost: the 2021 baseline showed $850M of wages against $2.82B of revenue, or roughly 30.1% of sales, while 2025 BLS wage data showed a $55,470 mean annual wage for employed locksmiths and safe repairers. Other major costs include locksets, cylinders, key blanks, electronic access hardware, automotive programming equipment, vehicles, fuel, insurance, licensing, dispatch software, local advertising, rent for shops, and card/payment fees. Profitability is modest in the baseline, with 2021 EBIT margin at 5.7%, reflecting heavy local competition and small-firm scale limits.
major_players: Liberty Safe and Security Products Inc
Fragmented independent locksmith shops and owner-operators
current_dynamics: The industry is balancing stable essential-service demand against weak housing turnover and uneven construction activity. Commercial work remains the largest revenue pool, but some discretionary upgrades are delayed when businesses or households face high financing and construction costs. Residential rekeying benefits from moves and renovations, yet 2025 existing-home sales stayed near historic lows. Electronic access control and smart locks are raising ticket sizes and technical requirements, while hardware stores, DIY smart-lock products, security alarm firms and integrated security providers pressure basic lock and key work.
whats_growing: Electronic access control, smart lock installation, app-based user provisioning, automotive transponder/fob programming, commercial master-key systems, institutional safe/vault service, property-management rekey programs, and recurring commercial maintenance are growing faster than basic mechanical lock work. Multifamily activity also helped parts of 2025 demand, with multifamily starts up 17.4% from 2024 even as single-family starts declined.
whats_shrinking: Basic key duplication, simple residential lock replacement, low-skill lockout calls and hardware resale are under pressure from self-service kiosks, big-box retailers, DIY smart-lock kits, online lock sales and roadside-assistance alternatives. Single-family new-construction-related demand weakened in 2025 as single-family starts fell 6.9% from 2024.
recent_developments: 2025-05: Census/HUD reported April 2025 housing starts at a 1.36M SAAR, with single-family starts down 12.0% year over year amid tariff, financing and cost uncertainty.
2025-06: IBISWorld's public market-size page listed 2025 US Locksmiths market size at $2.9B, 2025 growth at 1.3%, and 2020-2025 CAGR at -0.2%.
2026-01: NAR-reported data showed 2025 existing-home sales at about 4.061M, roughly flat with 2024 and the lowest annual level since 1995.
2026-02: NAHB reported 2025 total housing starts of 1.36M, down 0.6% from 2024, with single-family starts down 6.9% and multifamily starts up 17.4%.
2026-05: Census released final 2025 annual building permit estimates; NAHB cited 2025 permits of 1.43M, down 3.6% from 2024.
2026-06: BLS May 2025 OEWS data showed 15,040 employed locksmiths and safe repairers earning a mean $26.67 per hour and $55,470 per year.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is modestly positive but uneven. Demand should be steadier in emergency, automotive, institutional and commercial maintenance work than in housing-linked rekeying and new-installation work. A recovery in home sales or lower mortgage rates would lift residential rekey and renovation demand, while continued weakness in single-family construction would cap growth. The best-positioned operators are likely to be locksmiths that can install and maintain electronic access systems, integrate smart locks, handle automotive electronics, serve commercial accounts, and use digital dispatch and local search efficiently. The industry should remain fragmented, price-competitive and locally driven.

one_sentence: US locksmiths remain a small, mature and highly fragmented service industry, with 2025 revenue around $2.9B-$3.1B, modest near-term growth, and demand shifting from basic mechanical lock work toward electronic access control, smart locks and commercial security integration.
